evidence.auth_model: No vendor login or API key required for core durable-workflow functionality. DBOS is an open-source Python library (`pip install dbos`) that connects directly to a self-hosted or user-owned Postgres database via a connection string (env var `DBOS_SYSTEM_DATABASE_URL`) or a locally-run Postgres in Docker; docs quote: "Users can either provide their own connection string via the DBOS_SYSTEM_DATABASE_URL environment variable or start Postgres locally in Docker using DBOS tooling. No account or authentication is mentioned as necessary for local Postgres connectivity." The only login surface is the optional, separate "DBOS Conductor" cloud control plane: docs state "To connect your app to Conductor, first sign up for an account on the DBOS console" — that is opt-in and not required to use durable workflows/steps/queues. This satisfies C1 (no vendor login required; a Postgres instance the user already owns is the only dependency, not a paid API key).

evidence.fit_with_native_workflow: No native login/API key dependency (C1 satisfied via local Postgres, no vendor account for core use) and it is programmatically controllable via plain Python decorators rather than a CLI/exec surface, so it would sit as a library dependency inside a Python worker rather than as a peer harness (no MCP, no headless-exec mode documented). C3 isolation: each worktree/sandbox that owns its own Postgres connection string can own DBOS's durability state deterministically (no discovered global/shared state beyond the Postgres schema DBOS manages), matching the "C3 ownership" claim in the judges' fit-first reasoning. It is not a workflow/orchestration tool comparable to the Workflow tool or Claude Code's Agent tool; its relevant capability is durable resume of a long-lived Python worker process across crashes, which none of the listed incumbents (dagu's YAML scheduling, beads' task queue, worktrunk's worktrees, Temporal unqualified) currently provide as a lightweight decorator library with "no separate server process beyond Postgres."

evidence.isolation_model: No separate server process beyond Postgres: durability state (workflow/step checkpoints) is stored in the connected Postgres database from within the same process running the decorated Python code. README states: "DBOS is entirely contained in this open-source library, there's no additional infrastructure for you to configure or manage." A worktree/sandbox pointed at its own `DBOS_SYSTEM_DATABASE_URL` can own its own durability state; no hidden global state beyond that Postgres schema was found in the material read. Sandboxing/process isolation itself (e.g. container boundaries) is not something DBOS provides — it is orthogonal to the durable-workflow layer.

evidence.summary: DBOS Transact (Python) is an MIT-licensed, actively maintained (pushed today, release 3.0.0 nine days ago, roughly weekly release cadence, 1583 stars) decorator library that adds durable, resumable workflows to plain Python functions by checkpointing state to a Postgres database the user already owns — no vendor login, no separate orchestration server, no paid API key required for core use (only an optional cloud "Conductor" control plane needs a DBOS-console account, and that is opt-in). It has a tests/ directory and three GitHub Actions CI workflows (unit-test.yml, chaos-test.yml, publish.yml). All three judges independently converged on the same evidence-backed claim: DBOS's differentiator versus the shortlisted incumbents (dagu's YAML scheduling, beads' task queue, Temporal's unqualified server-based orchestration) is exact resume-from-last-completed-step for a long-lived Python worker process, achieved with no infrastructure beyond Postgres. No comparison has been executed in this session — every claim here is source_review from gh api calls and two docs.dbos.dev pages, not native_execution — so per the harness's promotion rule this stays a targeted_candidate / keep_but_compare, not adopted. The recommended acceptance path is a bounded local_integration test that kills and resumes a DBOS-based worker mid-step and asserts exactly-once resume, run against dagu (and optionally Temporal) as comparison arms; the exact test file path named by one judge (tests/durable/test_dbos_worker_resume.py) was not confirmed to exist upstream and would need to be authored as part of that protocol.

In an agent worktree, where worker code is edited between crash and restart, the restarted process recovers nothing by default — which is the exact scenario the fit claim is selling.

findings.problem: No `step()` wrapper API exists. The shipped mechanism is the string directives `"use workflow"` and `"use step"` processed by the `@workflow/swc-plugin` compiler. The docs record that a wrapper-based runtime API was prototyped and explicitly rejected, so the packet describes the design the project turned down. Only the `start()` half of the claim holds.

These directives trigger the `@workflow/swc-plugin` compiler". docs/how-it-works/understanding-directives.mdx:110 "Before settling on directives, we prototyped several other approaches... corrections: Corrected interface (C2): not a plain embeddable library. Durability is delivered by the `@workflow/swc-plugin` compiler transforming `"use workflow"` / `"use step"` directives at build time into two required bundles served as `POST /.well-known/workflow/v1/flow` and `POST /.well-known/workflow/v1/step`. Corrected fit (C2/C3): adopting this for `.claude/workflows/*.mjs` requires adding a bundler (Nitro/Rollup/Vite/Next) and an HTTP server to the harness, plus a World — not just restructuring code around the workflow/step split. Corrected auth (C1): the C1 conclusion stands — no Claude Code / Codex / GitHub / Google sign-in anywhere, and local plus Postgres self-hosting need no external account or API key (`WORKFLOW_TARGET_WORLD` + `DATABASE_URL` only). Replace the fabricated local-dev quote with docs/deploying/index.mdx:18, and replace the `VERCEL_DEPLOYMENT_ID` detail with the actual Vercel mechanism: OIDC tokens, `WORKFLOW_VERCEL_AUTH_TOKEN`, and CLI credentials from `vercel login`. Confirmed doc quotes, verified against the version-matched docs bundled in the 4.8.9 npm tarball rather than a summarized WebFetch — this closes the packet's second open_gap: "By default, steps have a maximum of 3 retry attempts before they fail and propagate the error to the workflow"; "the workflow code gets re-run multiple times during its lifecycle, each time using the event log to resume the workflow to the correct spot"; "no compute resources are used until the workflow resumes execution"; "The Local World stores workflow data in a `.workflow-data/` directory and processes steps synchronously"; "Managed queuing - Steps are processed reliably with automatic retries" / "Automatic scaling"; "does not have access to the Node.js runtime, and usable `npm` packages are limited"; "`Math.random` and `Date` constructors are fixed in workflow runs".

Still in-process, so deterministic code does not own the effects at OS level; effects run in the host app's process via step handlers.

Disposition unchanged in label, changed in reason: keep_but_compare, not targeted_candidate. The packet reached keep_but_compare on the grounds that no local comparison was executed; the stronger reason is that the documented architecture (mandatory bundler plus in-app HTTP routes) does not match the stated `.mjs` target, so the named comparison against dbos-transact-ts should be preceded by, or replaced with, a cheaper feasibility check. findings.claim: fit_with_native_workflow presents the remaining work as choosing a World and restructuring code around the step/workflow split.
findings.problem: It omits the load-bearing prerequisite. The expensive, failure-prone units in these graphs are `agent()` dispatches provided by the Claude Code Workflow runtime, not functions callable from a user-owned Node process; a durable-execution library can only checkpoint steps it itself invokes. Adopting `workflow` therefore presupposes re-hosting the orchestration on anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python (incumbent list: 'measured, not adopted') or `codex exec`. That prerequisite, not the World choice, is the actual cost of the fit.

The packet neither claims nor refutes this; it is unaddressed.

Automatic scaling' attributed to the Vercel World.

corrections: Rewrite fit_with_native_workflow: the package cannot be wired into `.claude/workflows/*` graphs at all — those are Claude Code Workflow-tool scripts run in a non-module `new Function` scope with `import()` forbidden by project contract (probe: FAIL 'Cannot use import statement outside a module'). The genuine .mjs files in that directory are short-lived deterministic CLIs with nothing to checkpoint. Any real fit requires first re-hosting orchestration on claude-agent-sdk-python (measured, not adopted) or `codex exec`, which is a larger decision than this packet's scope.

Rewrite overlap_with_incumbents to name the two incumbents actually holding the slot: (1) anthropics/claude-code's Workflow tool already resumes a failed or stopped run from cached agents (docs/native-token-workflow.md 'Failure and replay'; observed in docs/tasks/2026-09-21-native-ultracode.md:22,28-29); (2) dagu 2.16.6 (selected) already retries a persisted prior run at step granularity (`dagu retry --run-id=... --step=... --downstream`). Temporal/langgraph are the distant comparisons, not the near ones.

Correct the premise that the shortlist wants this capability: catalogs/foundation/manifest.json:250-259 records `worker-cancellation-crash-resume` as status accepted_within_scope with next_action 'do not rerun this fixture', and the same catalog's 2026-09-22 run refuted dbos-transact-py on exactly that gap-fit test (manifest-20260922.json adversarial_verification survives:false, both lenses refuted, high confidence; README.md:49 'refuted (no gap)'). A packet proposing the same capability class must either cite that record and argue it is wrong, or accept it.

Disposition: not_adopted for the stated fit (the named integration target is impossible as described), or at most keep_but_compare scoped to a different target — never targeted_candidate on the `.claude/workflows/*.mjs` framing.

Named comparison that would settle the remaining overlap question (the only one worth running): take one existing multi-stage graph, e.g. `.claude/workflows/review-changes.js`, and measure re-executed LLM stages after a kill at stage N. Arm 1 (incumbent, runnable today): run it, kill the client mid-stage, resume via `/workflows`, then `node $HOME/code/agent-lab/.claude/workflows/child-usage.mjs --latest` on the original and the resumed run and count re-dispatched children plus provider tokens. Arm 2 (incumbent, runnable today): wrap the same stages as `claude -p` steps in a dagu DAG, kill it, `dagu retry --run-id=<id> --step=<stage> --downstream`, count re-run steps. Arm 3 (candidate) is only constructible after the re-hosting prerequisite; a cheaper precursor is a bounded local_integration check in a scratch dir — `npm install workflow && npx workflow inspect runs` against a two-`step()` script that SIGKILLs itself between steps, then re-invoked — to confirm the event log skips the completed step with zero external account. Overturning finding 2/4 requires arm 3 re-running strictly fewer paid stages than arms 1 and 2 on the same kill point.

Out of lens, stated per instruction: the packet's repository-fact claims (stars, license, release cadence, 427 `.test.ts` matches, Cargo.toml) were not re-verified here; nothing in this review bears on C4.
